title: JOIN NOWHERE EXPEDITIONS!
summary:
Have your neighbours already packed and moved to Endros? **Maybe it's time YOU do too!**

**Nowhere Expeditions** recruits specialists willing to relocate to Endros and participate in expeditions beyond the Gates. 
Vacancies for researchers, engineers, physicians, sailors, security personnel, salvagers, artificers, surveyors and many other roles.  

**Is it hard to describe your qualifications on official paperwork?** We can let you shine... In Endros!

**Scared of the remoteness?** Sell your lord! Sell your house! Bring your family! Bring your sheep! Bring your cow! You can build a whole new life in Endros!

Be scared not! In Endros, you'll start anew, working at the pinnacle of science and helping lead the world into a new era. The Era of Magic!
details:
# History
It has been 11 years since the Valeoran Ruins were discovered at the far ends of an uncharted horizon. Rising from the sea and reaching high into the sky, fragments of an ancient wonder remain suspended, drifting in place over an unnaturally still ocean. Today, floating platforms, laboratories, workshops, shipyards and habitation blocks surround the ruins, forming Endros: a rapidly growing settlement so remote that newspapers have taken the liberty of calling it "Endros in the Middle of Nowhere", "Endwhere" or just "Nowhere".

Several years after the initial discovery, researchers observed portions of the ruins beginning to move, gathering together and forming temporary portals known as *Gates*. What lies beyond them varies widely: Ruins, Unknown Ecosystems, Impossible machinery. Strange places where familiar rules no longer apply and resources found nowhere else in the known world. Materials recovered from Gates have created an entirely new field of technology known as *Artificery*. More recently, researchers have begun documenting something even stranger: *Magic*.

# Game Details
New to the campaign? Read these rules in order; each one ends with a link to the next. The **Campaign** rules are required reading before your first expedition. The others are reference material you can look up when they come up in play.

{{reading-path}}

You can also browse every rule by topic in the [Rules](game.html#rules) section, and the [Archive](archive.html) for more lore.

title: Nowhere Expeditions
summary: Nowhere Expeditions is a Fate campaign about **Expeditioners**: specialists who gather in Endros, form crews, and go through the Gates to bring back whatever they can find. This is the first of four entries every new player should read.
details:
### Endros and the Gates

Endros is the expedition hub. Every expedition starts and ends there. Gates open into impossible environments, and Expeditioners go through them for knowledge, materials, artifacts, money and answers.

Your character is an Expeditioner. You don't play the settlement, a guild or a fixed party. You play one person who decides which risks are worth taking.

### There is no permanent party

Each expedition has its own crew, made up of the players who sign up for it. You might travel with completely different people from one session to the next.

### You choose what to pursue

Opportunities appear on the [Job Board](jobs.html): Gates to survey, objects to recover, problems to solve. The players choose which ones to take on. None of them are mandatory, and none of them wait for a plot to catch up.

### The world is persistent

What one crew discovers, damages, opens, or leaves unfinished stays that way for the next crew. Reports go into the [Archive](archive.html), and changes to the settlement appear on the [Outpost Sheet](outpost.html). A map drawn by one crew can save another crew's life.

### Play the way that suits you

There's no single right way to take part, and you don't need to attend every session. All of these are playing Nowhere Expeditions:

- joining expeditions through the Gates;
- working on Projects and Research between sessions;
- planning a Project with the GM and working out what it needs;
- roleplaying with other Expeditioners in Endros.

Do as much or as little of each as you enjoy. Each one changes the shared world in its own way.

### Between expeditions

Between expeditions your character has **Downtime**: time to work in Endros. Everything significant you do with it is a **Project Action**, whether you're building something, researching, recovering from an injury or repairing the settlement. The four-step Project Action is explained in [Downtime](game.html#post-downtime).

### You don't need to know the lore

You aren't expected to know the setting before you start. Knowledge is one of the main ways the campaign progresses: what the characters learn in play is a reward in itself. See *How Much Lore Should I Read?* in [Creating an Expeditioner](game.html#post-creating-an-expeditioner).

### Reading path for new players

1. **Nowhere Expeditions** (this entry)
2. [Creating an Expeditioner](game.html#post-creating-an-expeditioner)
3. [Expeditions](game.html#post-expeditions)
4. [Downtime](game.html#post-downtime)

Everything else is reference material you can look up when it comes up.

title: Creating an Expeditioner
summary: An Expeditioner is anyone with a reason to go through a Gate and a skill worth bringing. You don't need to be a fighter, and you don't need a long backstory: a clear idea of who you are, and why a crew would want you, is enough to start.
details:
### Start with three questions

- **Why are you in Endros?** Work, faith, debt, curiosity, exile, family, opportunity.
- **Why do you enter Gates?** What are you hoping to find, prove or escape?
- **Why would other Expeditioners want you in their crew?** This matters most in a campaign without a permanent party. Crews form around the skills a job needs.

Your answers become your **character concept**: one or two sentences that sum up who you are. For example, *"A disgraced harbor surveyor who maps Gates because nobody else will hire her"* or *"A field medic who keeps a ledger of every Expeditioner he couldn't save."*

### Specialists are encouraged

Characters don't need to be combat specialists. Cartographers, medics, linguists, riggers, cooks, mechanics and Gate scholars all earn their place on an expedition. Being excellent at one thing gives a crew a clear reason to invite you.

### Choose a Recruitment Faction

Most Expeditioners didn't simply appear in Endros on their own. A company, institution, government, employer, sponsor or personal arrangement usually helped them reach the Outpost and settle there.

Your **Recruitment Faction** represents that relationship.

- It grants a small **Extra**.
- It may decide who your character knows, what they can access and what others expect of them.
- It does **not** decide your profession, your Skills or your role on an expedition.

Choose one from the [Recruitment Factions](game.html#topic-recruitment-factions) topic on the Rules tab. If none of them fit your character, you can be **Independent**. Write your faction and its Extra in the Extras section of your character sheet.

### Your character sheet

Nowhere Expeditions uses Fate. The [character sheet](sheet.html) has a space for each of these. The detailed Fate rules explain how each one works in play.

- **Aspects** are short phrases that are true about your character, such as their concept, their trouble, a relationship or a belief. You invoke them for a bonus, and they can be compelled to complicate your life.
- **Skills** are what your character is good at, like Crafts, Lore, Notice or Physique, each with a rating. You roll them when the outcome is uncertain.
- **Stunts** are special tricks: narrow situations where your character gets a bonus or can do something unusual.
- **Stress and Consequences** show how much punishment your character can take. Stress is short-term and clears quickly. Consequences are lasting injuries or problems that need time and treatment. See [Consequences & Recovery](game.html#post-consequences-and-recovery).

### Equipment and your Personal Stash

Everything your character owns is kept in their **Personal Stash**. You buy equipment from the [Marketplace](marketplace.html) with **Coins**, and your Resources skill tops your Coins up after every expedition. You start with Coins equal to your Resources rating (none if it's +0 or lower). See [Coins, Marketplace & Personal Stash](game.html#post-coins-marketplace-and-personal-stash).

### Backstory

A few sentences are plenty. You don't need to know your character's whole history: things you discover in play can fill in the rest, and a blank space in your past can become a hook later.

### How Much Lore Should I Read?

Only read what your character would actually know. Pick the parts of the [Archive](archive.html) and the [Outpost Sheet](outpost.html) that relate to your concept and leave the rest for later.

- **A religion-focused character:** read about the faiths and folklore your character follows. Other beliefs can stay strange to you.
- **An artificer or engineer:** look at the [Marketplace](marketplace.html), the Facilities on the [Outpost Sheet](outpost.html), and [Resources](game.html#post-resources).
- **A Gate researcher:** read the Gate records in the Archive and the [Research](game.html#post-research) rules.
- **A newly arrived outsider:** read almost nothing. Your character doesn't know how Endros works yet, and finding out is part of playing them.

Not knowing things can suit your character, and discovering the world through play is intended. The Archive will still be there when your character needs it.

title: Expeditions
summary: An expedition is one crew taking on one job beyond a Gate, and every expedition session follows the same three parts: **Preparation**, **Exploration** and **Return**.

title: Downtime
summary: Downtime is the time your character has between expeditions. Every significant piece of work in Endros, whether building, researching, crafting or recovering, is a **Project**, and you spend Downtime on **Project Actions** to move Projects forward.
details:
### Gaining Downtime

Each time an expedition is completed, Expeditioners gain Downtime:

| Your character… | Downtime gained |
| --- | --- |
| took part in the expedition | **2** |
| did not take part (stayed in Endros) | **3** |

Characters who stayed behind spent the whole expedition in Endros, so they have a little more time for work at home. Missing a session doesn't mean falling behind: you can still help the settlement and your character between expeditions.

**You can hold at most 8 Downtime.** Any Downtime you would gain above 8 is lost, so spend it rather than saving it up.

Your current Downtime is shown at the top of your character's page. The GM keeps it up to date.

### Every Downtime Action is a Project Action

Anything significant you do between expeditions is treated as a Project: a goal with a Progress track that fills up as people work on it. Building a device, studying an artifact, repairing the harbor and healing a wound all work the same way.

**The Project Action:**

1. **Spend 1 Downtime.**
2. **Describe what your character does** and which Skill they use.
3. **Roll** against a difficulty the GM sets for that approach.
4. **Gain Progress:**

| Result | Progress |
| --- | --- |
| Fail | 0, and a Complication |
| Tie | 1 |
| Success | 2 |
| Success with Style | 3 |

When every Progress box is filled, the Project is complete and its effect happens. Projects can be your own, shared with other characters or open to all of Endros. See [Projects](game.html#post-projects) for the full rules.

> **Example.** Mira wants to understand the humming shard her crew brought back. That's a Research Project. She spends 1 Downtime, studies the shard with **Lore**, succeeds, and marks 2 Progress.

### Two limits

- **One action per Project between expeditions.** Your character can make only one Project Action on any single Project between two expeditions. To finish a big Project faster, spread it over several expeditions or get other characters to work on it too. Each of them can also make one action on it.
- **Outpost help costs 1 extra Downtime.** If one of Endros's Capabilities genuinely helps your action, you may spend 1 more Downtime on that action to add the Capability's rating to the Progress you gain. This is still one action on the Project. See [Outpost Capabilities](game.html#post-outpost-capabilities).

### What doesn't cost Downtime

Casual roleplay, conversations, visiting other characters, buying gear at the Marketplace and small fictional actions are free. Downtime is only for significant work that has a mechanical effect.

### Why Downtime is limited

Downtime keeps between-session play fair. A player who is very active between sessions gets more stories and scenes, but not unlimited mechanical progress. Everyone's characters have about the same amount of time to work with.

### Recovering from Consequences

Injuries and other lasting harm, to you or to Endros, don't fade on their own. Each one is removed with a **Recovery Project**, using these same Project Actions. See [Consequences & Recovery](game.html#post-consequences-and-recovery).

title: Nowhere Expeditions (the Company)
summary: **Nowhere Expeditions** is the name of this campaign, and also an in-world **company**: a recruitment and relocation agency that brings people from abroad to Endros and helps them settle in. Its recruits get the **Relocation Package**: +1 Coin after each expedition they take part in.

title: University of Verna
summary: The **University of Verna** is an academic institution with laboratories, archives and staff in Endros, and it sponsors scholars and field specialists to study the Gates. Its recruits get **Institutional Access**: +1 Progress on one Research Project Action between expeditions.

title: Independent
summary: **Independent** Expeditioners reached Endros on their own terms, without a major institution behind them. They owe nobody, and their own work comes first. **Self-Directed** gives them +1 Progress on one Personal Project Action between expeditions.

title: Projects
summary: A Project is work too big to settle with a single roll, such as building a machine, repairing a district or understanding an artifact. Every kind of significant between-expedition work uses the same Project framework and advances one Project Action at a time.
details:
### What a Project contains

| Part | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **Goal** | What the Project is trying to achieve. |
| **Type** | Personal, Public, Research and so on (see below). |
| **Progress** | How much work is needed, shown as boxes. The Project is complete when every box is filled. |
| **Requirements** | Things the Project needs in order to advance or finish. See [Project Requirements & Complications](game.html#post-project-requirements-and-complications). |
| **Relevant Outpost Capabilities** | The parts of Endros that can help. See [Outpost Capabilities](game.html#post-outpost-capabilities). |
| **Complications** | Problems that have come up along the way. |
| **Completion Effect** | What changes when the Project is complete. |

Projects appear on the [Outpost Sheet](outpost.html) and in each character's Projects tab.

### Project Types

These are all the same system applied to different goals, not separate rules.

- **Personal Project:** your own work, usually for your character. See [Personal Stash & Crafting](game.html#post-personal-stash-and-crafting).
- **Public Project:** work for Endros that any character can contribute to.
- **Research Project:** answering a question. See [Research](game.html#post-research).
- **Marketplace Project:** making an item generally available. See [Marketplace Development](game.html#post-marketplace-development).
- **Facility Project:** adding a Facility to Endros. See [Facilities & Outpost Development](game.html#post-facilities-and-outpost-development).
- **Recovery / Repair Project:** fixing damage or a lasting problem. See [Consequences & Recovery](game.html#post-consequences-and-recovery).

### The Project Action

Every Downtime Action is a Project Action (see [Downtime](game.html#post-downtime)). **Spend 1 Downtime**, then tell the GM:

1. what your character is doing;
2. which Skill they are using;
3. how that approach moves the Project forward.

The GM sets a difficulty based on how dangerous, uncertain or ambitious **that approach** is. Roll, and gain Progress:

| Result | Progress |
| --- | --- |
| **Fail** | 0, and a Complication is created |
| **Tie** | 1 |
| **Success** | 2 |
| **Success with Style** | 3 |

**Capability support:** if one of Endros's Capabilities genuinely helps with what you are doing, you may spend **1 extra Downtime** on the action to add that Capability's rating to the Progress gained. Only **one** Capability can support a single Project Action. See [Outpost Capabilities](game.html#post-outpost-capabilities).

**One action per Project between expeditions:** each character can make only one Project Action on a given Project between two expeditions. Spending extra Downtime for Capability support doesn't count as a second action.

> **Example.** Tomas works on *Restore the Harbor Crane*. He uses **Crafts** to rebuild the gearbox using the Workshops' tools, and spends 2 Downtime: 1 for the action and 1 so Endros's **Industry** supports it. The GM sets the difficulty at Fair (+2). Tomas succeeds: 2 Progress, plus Industry's rating. He can't work on the crane again until after the next expedition, but other characters can.

### Bigger Projects aren't harder to roll

A powerful Project shouldn't simply have a higher difficulty. Ambitious Projects instead need:

- more Progress;
- Requirements;
- several stages;
- specialized Facilities;
- recovered Resources;
- discoveries;
- expedition objectives.

### Project size (GM guidelines)

| Size | Progress |
| --- | --- |
| Minor | about 4 |
| Standard | about 6 |
| Major | about 10 |
| Grand | about 15 or more, or several stages |

These are guidelines for the GM. A Project can be bigger or smaller if the situation calls for it.

title: Project Requirements & Complications
summary: Two things can stop or change a Project: **Requirements**, which are things the Project needs, and **Complications**, which are new problems that come up while you work on it.
details:
### Requirement or Complication?

- **Requirement:** something the Project needs. It may be known from the start or found out while you work.
- **Complication:** a new problem caused by the work, usually after a failed or risky Project Action.

### Requirements

A Requirement is a known condition the Project needs. Common kinds:

| Requirement | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Resource** | A Resource with the `Conduct` Function (see [Resource Functions](game.html#post-resource-functions)). |
| **Facility** | A containment lab to work safely. |
| **Knowledge** | Finished Research on how the artifact reacts to heat. |
| **Capability** | Endros's Medicine at a certain rating. |
| **Specialist / NPC** | A glassblower willing to work on Gate material. |
| **Previous Project** | The harbor must be repaired first. |
| **Expedition** | A sample has to be brought back from a specific Gate. |
| **Consequence slot** | Recovering a personal Severe Consequence needs a free Moderate slot (see [Consequences & Recovery](game.html#post-consequences-and-recovery)). |

If a Requirement is missing, the Project may be **Paused**. You can't advance it until that need is met. A Paused Project keeps its Progress.

### Complications

Complications should create new problems to deal with, not simply wipe out Progress. A Complication might be:

- a new **Aspect** attached to the Project, such as *Unstable Prototype* or *The Foreman Has Doubts*;
- a problem that makes future Project Actions harder;
- a **Blocking Complication** that pauses the Project until it is resolved;
- extra Progress needed;
- a new material or knowledge Requirement;
- an **expedition objective**.

> **Example.** A failed Project Action on *Calibrate the Resonance Lens* cracks the only lens. The GM adds a Complication: *Replacement lens glass must be recovered from the Gate where the original was found.* That becomes a new listing on the Job Board.

Complications that lead to expeditions are especially valuable. They send work from the Settlement Loop back into the Expedition Loop and give crews a reason to go somewhere.

When a Complication is resolved, the Project records how it was dealt with.

title: Research
summary: Research is a Project whose goal is an answer. It uses the same Downtime, Project Action and Progress rules as every other Project and doesn't have a separate system.

title: Outpost Capabilities
summary: Capabilities describe what Endros can reliably support as a settlement. Each has a rating on the [Outpost Sheet](outpost.html), and a Capability can add Progress when the settlement's people, tools or expertise genuinely help your Project.
details:
### The six Capabilities

| Capability | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| **Industry** | Crafting, repairs and manufacturing. |
| **Research** | Investigation, analysis and Gate knowledge. |
| **Commerce** | Trade, funding and access to resources. |
| **Security** | Defense, policing and emergency response. |
| **Medicine** | Treatment and recovery. |
| **Infrastructure** | Facilities, transportation and services. |

The Outpost Sheet also lists the Facilities and characters behind each Capability: the workshops, laboratories and docks that do the work.

### Capabilities in Project Actions

When you make a Project Action (see [Projects](game.html#post-projects)), you may **spend 1 extra Downtime** to have one relevant Capability **add its rating to the Progress you gain**, as long as the settlement is actually helping you.

- Rebuilding an engine in the Workshops: **Industry** helps.
- Rebuilding it alone in a tent at the edge of a Gate: Industry probably doesn't help.

A Capability isn't an automatic solution. You still describe what your character is doing and roll a Skill. The Capability adds to the result. Only one Capability can support each Project Action, and the extra Downtime doesn't count as a second action on the Project.

> **Example.** Mira studies a preserved Gate organism in the University laboratories. She spends 2 Downtime: 1 for the action and 1 for the laboratory's help. She rolls Lore and succeeds for 2 Progress, then adds Endros's Research rating because the laboratory's equipment and staff are part of her approach.

### Capabilities as Requirements

Advanced Projects may need a Capability at a certain rating before they can start or finish. For example, a surgical procedure on a Gate-touched patient might need a certain level of Medicine. See [Project Requirements & Complications](game.html#post-project-requirements-and-complications).

### Improving Capabilities

Capabilities can change over time. Facilities and completed Projects can improve them, and Outpost Consequences can strain them. See [Facilities & Outpost Development](game.html#post-facilities-and-outpost-development).

title: Consequences & Recovery
summary: Consequences are lasting harm, to your character or to Endros. In this campaign they don't fade with time: you work them off with **Recovery Projects**, and each finished Recovery Project makes the Consequence one step less severe.
details:
### This replaces Fate's recovery rules

In standard Fate, a Consequence clears after enough time passes once recovery starts. **Nowhere Expeditions doesn't use that rule.** A Consequence, whether personal or on the Outpost, stays until a Recovery Project lowers it.

### Severity sets the Progress

A Recovery Project needs as much Progress as the Consequence's severity:

| Personal Consequence | Outpost Consequence | Progress needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mild | Low | 2 |
| Moderate | Moderate | 4 |
| Severe | High | 6 |
| — | Critical | 8 |

### Each Recovery Project lowers it one step

Completing a Recovery Project doesn't remove the Consequence outright. It brings it down **one tier**:

- Severe becomes Moderate, Moderate becomes Mild, and a Mild Consequence is removed.
- On the Outpost, Critical becomes High, High becomes Moderate, Moderate becomes Low, and a Low Consequence is removed.

Rewrite the Consequence to fit its new severity and move it into that slot. Then start a new Recovery Project for the next step if you want to keep going.

### The lower slot must be free

A personal Consequence can only step down into an **empty** slot, so each personal Recovery Project has a Requirement (see [Project Requirements & Complications](game.html#post-project-requirements-and-complications)):

| Recovering a… | Requires a free… |
| --- | --- |
| Severe Consequence | Moderate slot |
| Moderate Consequence | Mild slot |
| Mild Consequence | nothing; it is simply removed |

If the slot below is taken, the Recovery Project is **Paused** until it is free. Usually that means recovering the lighter Consequence first.

This applies only to personal Consequences. The Outpost has no slot limits, so its Consequences can always step down.

> **Example.** Tomas comes back from a Gate with the Severe Consequence ***Shattered Leg*** and the Moderate Consequence ***Cracked Ribs***. His Moderate slot is taken, so the leg has to wait.
>
> 1. **Strap the Ribs** (4 Progress, needs his Mild slot free, which it is). The ribs become Mild: ***Sore Ribs***. His Moderate slot is now free.
> 2. **Set the Bone** (6 Progress). The leg becomes Moderate: ***Leg in a Splint***.
> 3. **Rest the Ribs** (2 Progress). ***Sore Ribs*** is removed, which frees his Mild slot.
> 4. **Learn to Walk on It Again** (4 Progress). The leg becomes Mild: ***Stiff Knee***.
> 5. **Back to Full Strength** (2 Progress). The last Consequence is gone.

### Working on a Recovery Project

Recovery uses the normal Project Action (see [Downtime](game.html#post-downtime) and [Projects](game.html#post-projects)), including the one-action-per-Project limit between expeditions.

- **The approach has to make sense.** A broken leg needs setting and rest, and a shaken mind needs help or resolution. The GM may require a suitable Facility, an NPC healer or particular circumstances.
- **Others can help.** A crewmate who is a field medic can spend their own Downtime on your Recovery Project. Each character can still make only one action on it between expeditions.
- **Medicine** (for people) or another fitting Capability (for the Outpost) can support an action for 1 extra Downtime. See [Outpost Capabilities](game.html#post-outpost-capabilities).

### Outpost Consequences

When Endros's stress track is full, the settlement takes a Consequence, recorded on the [Outpost Sheet](outpost.html). Its Recovery Project is a **Public Project**: anyone can work on it.

> **Example.** Endros takes the High Consequence ***Industrial District Damaged***.
>
> **Repair the Industrial District**: Public Recovery Project, 6 Progress, supported by Industry or Infrastructure. When it's complete, the Consequence drops to Moderate, for example ***Industrial District Running at Half Capacity***.

### Consequences are opportunities too

An Outpost Consequence should be more than a penalty. A damaged district means displaced workers, missing supplies, salvage opportunities and maybe someone who caused it. All of these are things to investigate, fix or take advantage of.

title: Coins, Marketplace & Personal Stash
summary: Your character's equipment lives in their **Personal Stash**. You buy it at the Marketplace with **Coins**, your **Resources** skill tops your Coins up after every expedition, and before each expedition you choose what to carry, up to your **carry limit** (6 by default).
details:
### Coins

Your Coins are shown on your character's page and on your [character sheet](sheet.html).

- **Starting Coins:** a new Expeditioner starts with Coins equal to their Resources rating (none if it's +0 or lower).
- **Buying:** pay an item's [Marketplace](marketplace.html) price (its sale price, if it's discounted) and add it to your Personal Stash.
- Buying doesn't cost Downtime.
- **Availability:** an item's availability (Common, Restricted or Rare) doesn't change its price. Only items marked *Unavailable* can't be bought right now.
- **Rewards:** jobs and the GM can also give you Coins.

### Resources refreshes your Coins

After each expedition, every Expeditioner **refreshes** their Coins against their **Resources** skill:

- If you have **fewer** Coins than your Resources rating, raise them to that rating.
- If you have **as many or more**, keep what you have.
- If your character **took part** in the expedition, refresh first, **then** add any reward Coins.

A Resources rating of +0 or lower doesn't refresh anything.

> **Example.** Ines spent all her Coins and has Resources at Fair (+2). The next expedition ends, so she refreshes to **2**. Tomas also had 0 Coins and has Resources at Average (+1). He was on that expedition, which paid each crew member 3 Coins. He refreshes to 1, then adds the reward, for **4** Coins.

### Your Personal Stash

Your Personal Stash holds everything your character owns: what you bought, what Projects made for you (see [Personal Stash & Crafting](game.html#post-personal-stash-and-crafting)) and what you were given. It's listed on your character's page.

### Bringing Gear on an expedition

During Preparation (see [Expeditions](game.html#post-expeditions)), mark the items you're taking as **Brought into action**.

- Their total weight (each item's weight × how many you bring) can be at most your **carry limit**.
- Your carry limit is **6** by default. A stunt can raise it, and some situations can lower it. Set it on your character sheet when that happens.
- Each item's weight is listed in the Marketplace.

**Weight isn't how heavy something is.** It combines size, bulk, fragility, upkeep and how awkward the item is to keep at hand: how hard it is to bring with you. A sheet of paper can weigh more than a hammer if it has to stay perfectly dry.

> **Example.** Mira brings a climbing kit (weight 3), two lanterns (weight 1 each) and a field journal (weight 0): 5 of her 6. A second climbing kit would put her over the limit.

### Forgot something?

Gear you didn't bring isn't completely out of reach. During the expedition, you can declare that you had an item from your Personal Stash with you after all:

| If adding it would… | It costs |
| --- | --- |
| keep you **within** your carry limit | **1 stress**, on a stress track of your choice |
| take you **over** your carry limit | **1 Fate Point** |

Mark the item as brought into action. It stays with you for the rest of the expedition. You can only produce items you own: anything not in your Personal Stash is still back in Endros, or still in the Marketplace.

> **Example.** Halfway up a cliff, Mira realises she left her second rope behind. She is carrying 5 of her 6 and the rope weighs 1, so she takes 1 stress and the rope was in her pack all along. Later she wants her climbing kit too (weight 3, which would bring her to 9), so she spends a Fate Point.

### Keeping your sheet up to date

Use your [character sheet](sheet.html) for everything above:

- the **Coins** counter;
- **Buy** buttons in its Marketplace tab, which take the price from your Coins;
- **Brought into action** checkboxes, with your carried weight shown against your carry limit;
- the **carry limit** itself, which you can change when a stunt or situation calls for it.

Press **Save file** and send the file to the GM, who brings the changes into the campaign records.

title: Resources
summary: A **Resource** is anything useful recovered from a Gate, such as a material, organism, substance or component. Whoever discovers a new Resource **names it**, and its **Functions** decide what it can be used to build.
details:
### You name what you discover

When Expeditioners bring back a Resource nobody has recorded before, **they name it**. If a whole crew found it together, the crew agrees on the name. From then on, everyone in Endros knows it by that name.

> **Example.** Tomas's crew brings back glassy shards that stay warm for days and flare when struck. They call them **Emberglass**, and that is the name every crew uses afterwards.

Materials invented through Material Engineering are named by the people who make them (see [Material Engineering](game.html#post-material-engineering)).

### What a Resource has

| | What it is | Example (Weeping Iron) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Description** | What it looks and feels like. This is fiction only. | Dense, reddish and metallic. |
| **Functions** | What it can **do**: reusable properties that Projects ask for. | `Reinforce`, `Regenerate` |
| **Special Properties** | Odd behavior too specific to be a Function. | Slowly bends towards exposed blood. |

Functions are the part that matters for crafting. The full list, and how Functions combine, is in [Resource Functions](game.html#post-resource-functions).

### Known and Hidden Functions

Some Functions are obvious as soon as a Resource is recovered. Others are **Hidden**: they're already in the material, but nobody understands them well enough to use them yet. [Research](game.html#post-research) can reveal Hidden Functions, so a Resource brought back long ago can suddenly become valuable.

### Projects ask for Functions

Projects usually ask for Resources with particular Functions instead of a specific named material (see [Project Requirements & Complications](game.html#post-project-requirements-and-complications)). Any known Resource with those Functions will do, whichever Gate it came from. Different discoveries can solve the same problem in different ways.

title: Resource Functions
summary: **Functions** are the shared vocabulary of crafting and artificery. Each one is a verb describing what a Resource can **do**: `Store`, `Conduct`, `Phase`. Projects ask for Functions, and how two Functions interact tells you whether combining them will be easy, hard or dangerous.
details:
### Functions are capabilities, not appearance

A Function is an exceptional, technologically useful property. It isn't a description.

- A crystal isn't automatically `Refract`, and a heavy material isn't automatically `Anchor`.
- A biological material isn't automatically `Regenerate`.
- **Ordinary materials don't have Functions.** Steel is durable, but ordinary steel isn't a `Reinforce` Resource. Functions are for properties remarkable enough to matter in artificery.

Strange behavior too specific to be a Function is a **Special Property** instead (see [Resources](game.html#post-resources)). Not every oddity deserves a new Function.

### How many Functions?

| Functions | Typically means |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | a fairly simple Resource |
| 2 | a normal, interesting Gate Resource |
| 3 | an unusually valuable Resource |
| 4 or more | an exceptional material |

This is a guideline, not a limit.

### Reading a Requirement

Projects ask for Functions, not named materials (see [Project Requirements & Complications](game.html#post-project-requirements-and-complications)):

> **Material Requirement:** a Resource with `Store` and `Conduct`.

Requirements can offer choices:

> Requires `Stabilize` and either `Insulate` or `Nullify`.

Any known Resource that has the Functions will do. When you offer one, explain how it solves the engineering problem: why *this* material, used *this* way, does the job.

### How Functions interact

| Interaction | Example | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Synergy** | `Conduct` + `Store` | The Functions support each other. The combination is comparatively easy to engineer. It doesn't give extra Progress. |
| **Opposition** | `Conduct` + `Insulate` | The Functions work against each other. It isn't impossible, but it may need clever design, extra Requirements, Research or a specialized Facility. |
| **Instability** | `Catalyze` + `Release` | The Functions interact in dangerous or unpredictable ways. These combinations aren't forbidden. Getting one under control can lead to advanced technology. |

The Function table below names the specific problem in brackets:

- labels like **[Cancellation]**, **[Suppression]** or **[Strain]** mark an Opposition;
- labels like **[Runaway]**, **[Overload]** or **[Rupture]** mark an Instability.

A pair can be both. `Store` and `Release` work well together, but discharge catastrophically if uncontrolled.

For a difficult combination, the GM may set:

- a higher difficulty;
- extra Resource Requirements, or a Catalyst;
- a Facility or Research Requirement;
- several Project stages;
- harsher Complications on failure.

**These relationships are engineering guidance, not a chemistry table.** The same combination can behave differently depending on the Resources involved, what you're building, the Facilities and Research available, and your method. The GM decides how a specific combination behaves.

### The Functions

| Function | What it does | Example uses | Common synergies | Difficult / dangerous pairings |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Absorb** | Draws energy, force, substances, or other phenomena into itself. | Protective armor, collectors, filters, energy harvesting | `Store`, `Dampen`, `Regenerate` | `Release` **[Runaway]**, `Amplify` **[Overload]**, `Nullify` **[Cancellation]** |
| **Adapt** | Changes its behavior or structure in response to conditions. | Adaptive armor, environmental gear, self-adjusting machines | `Sense`, `Regenerate`, `Record`, `Flex` | `Stabilize` **[Opposition]**, `Nullify` **[Cancellation]**, `Transmute` **[Runaway]** |
| **Amplify** | Increases the strength of an existing signal, force, or effect. | Weapons, sensors, transmitters, power systems | `Conduct`, `Resonate`, `Release`, `Sense` | `Dampen` **[Cancellation]**, `Nullify` **[Cancellation]**, `Store` **[Overload]** |
| **Anchor** | Resists movement, displacement, distortion, or dimensional change. | Gate anchors, foundations, containment systems, dimensional restraints | `Reinforce`, `Stabilize`, `Insulate`, `Bind` | `Phase` **[Opposition]**, `Lighten` **[Strain]**, `Transmute` **[Strain]** |
| **Bind** | Joins substances, structures, or effects and helps them remain integrated. | Composite materials, repairs, artificial organs, multi-material equipment | `Reinforce`, `Flex`, `Stabilize`, `Catalyze` | `Phase` **[Separation]**, `Transmute` **[Instability]**, `Release` **[Rupture]** |
| **Catalyze** | Enables or accelerates another reaction or transformation. | Material synthesis, refining, medicine, artificery | `Transmute`, `Regenerate`, `Adapt`, `Bind` | `Nullify` **[Cancellation]**, `Stabilize` **[Opposition]**, `Release` **[Runaway]** |
| **Conduct** | Transfers energy, magic, heat, signals, or similar phenomena efficiently. | Wiring, power systems, weapons, artificery circuits | `Store`, `Release`, `Amplify`, `Sense` | `Insulate` **[Opposition]**, `Nullify` **[Cancellation]**, `Amplify` **[Overload risk]** |
| **Dampen** | Reduces the intensity of forces, signals, vibrations, or magical effects. | Shock absorbers, silencers, protective gear, anomaly shielding | `Absorb`, `Insulate`, `Stabilize`, `Anchor` | `Amplify` **[Cancellation]**, `Resonate` **[Suppression]**, `Release` **[Pressure buildup]** |
| **Flex** | Deforms substantially without losing integrity and can recover its shape. | Flexible armor, springs, joints, climbing gear, shock protection | `Adapt`, `Reinforce`, `Lighten`, `Bind` | `Anchor` **[Strain]**, `Stabilize` **[Reduced function]** |
| **Insulate** | Prevents or greatly reduces the transfer of energy or another phenomenon. | Protective suits, containment walls, thermal barriers, magic shielding | `Dampen`, `Store`, `Stabilize`, `Anchor` | `Conduct` **[Opposition]**, `Release` **[Rupture risk]**, `Amplify` **[Containment failure]** |
| **Lighten** | Reduces effective mass, weight, or inertia. | Vehicles, portable machinery, armor, lifting systems | `Flex`, `Phase`, `Reinforce` | `Anchor` **[Opposition]**, `Store` **[Instability at high load]** |
| **Nullify** | Suppresses or cancels a specific phenomenon or active effect. | Anti-magic equipment, containment, interference devices, anomaly suppression | `Dampen`, `Anchor`, `Insulate` | `Amplify` **[Cancellation]**, `Resonate` **[Cancellation]**, `Regenerate` **[Suppression]**, `Catalyze` **[Suppression]** |
| **Phase** | Allows matter or effects to partially leave normal physical interaction or cross boundaries. | Barrier penetration, dimensional equipment, Gate technology, exotic transport | `Lighten`, `Refract`, `Sense` | `Anchor` **[Direct opposition]**, `Bind` **[Separation]**, `Reinforce` **[Structural strain]** |
| **Record** | Retains information, patterns, impressions, or states. | Memory storage, sensors, autonomous devices, research equipment | `Sense`, `Resonate`, `Adapt`, `Store` | `Transmute` **[Corruption]**, `Nullify` **[Erasure]**, `Regenerate` **[Replication of errors]** |
| **Refract** | Redirects, bends, splits, or focuses waves, light, energy, or magical phenomena. | Lenses, sensors, beam weapons, camouflage, magical optics | `Sense`, `Resonate`, `Conduct`, `Phase` | `Nullify` **[Cancellation]**, `Amplify` **[Focusing hazard]**, `Release` **[Discharge hazard]** |
| **Regenerate** | Repairs, regrows, or restores damaged structure. | Medicine, living materials, self-repairing armor, sustainable machinery | `Adapt`, `Record`, `Reinforce`, `Absorb` | `Transmute` **[Runaway growth]**, `Nullify` **[Suppression]**, `Catalyze` **[Runaway]** |
| **Reinforce** | Increases structural durability, toughness, or resistance to damage. | Armor, buildings, tools, pressure vessels | `Anchor`, `Bind`, `Flex`, `Stabilize` | `Phase` **[Fracture risk]**, `Lighten` **[Engineering strain]** |
| **Release** | Emits stored energy, force, matter, or another accumulated effect. | Engines, weapons, propulsion, emergency systems | `Store`, `Conduct`, `Amplify`, `Refract` | `Insulate` **[Rupture]**, `Catalyze` **[Runaway]**, `Absorb` **[Feedback]**, `Store` **[Overload if uncontrolled]** |
| **Resonate** | Responds strongly to particular frequencies, patterns, signals, or magical signatures. | Communications, Gate detectors, scanners, tuned devices | `Sense`, `Amplify`, `Record`, `Refract` | `Dampen` **[Suppression]**, `Nullify` **[Cancellation]**, `Stabilize` **[Detuning]** |
| **Sense** | Detects a particular substance, condition, force, or phenomenon. | Detectors, medical diagnostics, Gate scanners, environmental equipment | `Record`, `Adapt`, `Resonate`, `Refract` | `Nullify` **[Blindness]**, `Dampen` **[Signal loss]**, `Amplify` **[Overload risk]** |
| **Stabilize** | Keeps a substance, state, reaction, or phenomenon predictable and resistant to unwanted change. | Reactor housings, containment, precision equipment, volatile materials | `Store`, `Anchor`, `Reinforce`, `Insulate` | `Adapt` **[Opposition]**, `Transmute` **[Opposition]**, `Catalyze` **[Opposition]**, `Resonate` **[Detuning]** |
| **Store** | Holds energy, substances, information, or another phenomenon for later use. | Batteries, reservoirs, memory media, magical accumulators | `Absorb`, `Conduct`, `Stabilize`, `Release`, `Record` | `Amplify` **[Overload]**, `Release` **[Catastrophic discharge if uncontrolled]**, `Transmute` **[Containment instability]** |
| **Transmute** | Changes matter, structure, or properties into another form. | Refining, fabrication, alchemy, advanced artificery, recycling | `Catalyze`, `Adapt`, `Bind` | `Stabilize` **[Opposition]**, `Regenerate` **[Runaway transformation]**, `Record` **[Pattern corruption]**, `Anchor` **[Structural conflict]** |

### Example Resources

The same Function turns up in very different materials:

| Resource | Functions | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Emberglass** | `Store`, `Release` · Hidden: `Resonate` | Warm glassy shards that flare when struck. `Store` and `Release` work together, but it can discharge catastrophically if mishandled. |
| **Whisper Silk** | `Flex`, `Insulate`, `Record` | Pale thread that keeps the sound of anything spoken near it. |
| **Anchorstone** | `Anchor`, `Stabilize`, `Reinforce` | Grey stone that refuses to drift. All three Functions support each other, which makes it ideal for foundations. |
| **Mimic Resin** | `Adapt`, `Record`, `Regenerate` | Amber gel that remembers a shape, takes it on and repairs itself into it. Combining `Record` and `Regenerate` risks replicating errors: a crack it "remembers" grows back. |

### Random Resource

Need a Resource for a Gate, an experiment or inspiration? Draw some Functions at random:

To go further, see [Material Engineering](game.html#post-material-engineering) for making new materials and [Research](game.html#post-research) for uncovering Hidden Functions.

title: Material Engineering
summary: When no known Resource has the Functions a Project needs, an artificer, engineer or researcher can try to **make one**. Material Engineering is optional advanced play for characters who enjoy invention.

title: Personal Stash & Crafting
summary: A Personal Project can create, modify or restore an item for your character. When it is finished, the item goes into your **Personal Stash**, but making one working item doesn't make it available to everyone in Endros.
details:
### Making an item

Use a Personal Project (see [Projects](game.html#post-projects)) to:

- **create** a new item;
- **modify** an item you already have;
- **restore** a damaged item or an artifact.

The Project's Requirements often include Resources with particular Functions (see [Resource Functions](game.html#post-resource-functions)). When the Project is complete, the item is added to your **Personal Stash**, and it counts towards your carry limit like any other Gear (see [Coins, Marketplace & Personal Stash](game.html#post-coins-marketplace-and-personal-stash)).

### One item is not a product line

Creating a working item gives **you** that item. It doesn't mean Endros can make more.

> **Example.** Ines finishes a Personal Project and creates **Gate-Silk Armor**. She owns the prototype and can wear it on her next expedition. Nobody else can buy Gate-Silk Armor yet.
>
> If the crews want it to become generally available, someone needs to start a **Marketplace Project**, and Ines's prototype might be one of its Requirements.

### Summary

| Project | Result |
| --- | --- |
| **Personal Project** | One item, in your Personal Stash. |
| **Marketplace Project** | The item can be bought by everyone. See [Marketplace Development](game.html#post-marketplace-development). |

title: Marketplace Development
summary: A **Marketplace Project** is Endros learning to reliably make, acquire or distribute an item. When it is finished, the item appears in the [Marketplace](marketplace.html) and any Expeditioner can get it there.

title: Facilities & Outpost Development
summary: A Facility is a permanent addition to Endros, such as a laboratory, hospital wing or workshop, and it is usually built through a **Public Project** that many characters work on across many expeditions.
details:
### How a Facility gets built

1. **Someone proposes it** and explains what it is for.
2. **The GM defines its Completion Effect**: what Endros can do once it exists.
3. **Requirements are set** (see [Project Requirements & Complications](game.html#post-project-requirements-and-complications)).
4. **Players spend Downtime** on Project Actions (see [Projects](game.html#post-projects)).
5. **Missing Requirements** may lead to Research or expedition objectives.
6. **When the Project is complete**, the Facility joins Endros and appears on the [Outpost Sheet](outpost.html).

### What Facilities do

Facilities should mostly create **new possibilities** rather than just add numbers. A Facility might:

- unlock new kinds of Project;
- allow safe work with dangerous materials;
- meet Requirements for other Projects;
- unlock new Marketplace items;
- offer special Preparation actions before expeditions;
- make recovery possible for certain Consequences;
- improve or expand an Outpost Capability (see [Outpost Capabilities](game.html#post-outpost-capabilities));
- allow Research that was impossible before.

> **Example: a Containment Laboratory.**
> - **Proposed because:** nobody can safely study Resources that combine `Catalyze` and `Release`. Two samples have already exploded in the University.
> - **Type:** Public Project (Facility), Major, about 10 Progress
> - **Requirements:** Research at a set rating; a shielding material with `Stabilize` and either `Insulate` or `Nullify`; a qualified overseer
> - **Completion Effect:** Projects that handle unstable Resources can be worked on safely in Endros, and it adds a Research Capability asset.

### A shared achievement

Because a Public Project is open to everyone, a Facility is usually built by many players over several expeditions. One character proposes it, another crew brings back the shielding, and someone who has missed three sessions spends their extra Downtime finishing it. Whoever completes it, the result is part of Endros for every crew that follows.
